title: Overview and justification
body:
This course is about presenting with authority and collaborating well: the harder half of presenting, once you already know how to build and deliver a talk. By the end you will be able to present with authority and defend your argument, collaborate effectively in group work, and articulate what both are worth to you as a graduate.

These are not polish. The ability to hold a room, answer a hostile question, and work through conflict in a team is exactly what employers test at interview and what professional life demands daily. It is also where the strongest marks, and the real confidence, are found.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: present with authority, asserting and defending your argument with an academic voice
collaborate effectively in group work, drawing on the behaviours tutors and employers value
handle conflict and articulate the value of presenting and group work to your development as a graduate.

title: In real academic practice
body: Presenting and group work are where your degree meets professional life most directly. Every pitch, every meeting where views clash, every time you must win a room rather than simply inform it, draws on these skills. Build authority and collaboration now and they carry into interviews, into the teams you will join, and into the judgement your profession will expect of you.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, presenting with authority: owning your material and defending your argument. Second, collaborating in group work: why the process matters and what tutors look for. Third, conflict and value: using an awareness of personality to resolve disputes, and articulating what the experience is worth. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Confidence check
instruction: Before you start, rate how confident you feel about each statement. There are no right or wrong answers.
_preConfirmation: Thank you. You will see these statements again at the end of the course, so you can see how your confidence has changed.

_items.text: I can present with authority and defend my argument when questioned.
I can collaborate effectively in a group and show the behaviours tutors value.
I can handle conflict in a team and articulate the value of presenting and group work.

title: Orientation
body: You already know how to build a presentation and deliver it across different formats. The step that separates a competent presenter from an authoritative one is harder to pin down. It is the sense that the room belongs to you, that you own your material rather than recite it, and that a difficult question is something you welcome. This lesson is about that step.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are expected to do more than survive a presentation. The aim is to command it: to speak as the person who knows this material best in the room, and to defend your argument when it is challenged. That is a high bar, and it is reached through preparation and practice, not through personality.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain what it means to present with authority: owning your material rather than reciting it
recognise an academic voice that asserts and defends an argument in a worked example
choose an authoritative response to a difficult question about a presentation in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Presenting with authority does not mean being loud or polished. It means owning your material: knowing it well enough that you can speak to it rather than read it, and stand behind the argument you are making. A presentation is not a recital of facts. It is a case you put to an audience, and authority is the confidence, earned through preparation, to put that case and then defend it.

This is why the questions that follow a presentation matter so much. Answering a challenge well shows that the argument is yours, not borrowed. Developing this is how you build an academic voice: the ability to assert a position and hold it up under scrutiny, which is what university, and later your profession, rewards.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about the last presentation you gave. Were you reciting your slides, or could you have defended your argument if someone had pushed back? What is one thing you could do next time to present with more authority?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Presenting with authority means owning your material rather than reciting it, and standing behind your argument when it is challenged. You can now explain what authority looks like, recognise it in how a presenter handles a question, and choose an authoritative response yourself. The next lesson turns from the individual to the team, and the skills collaboration asks of you.

instruction: This lesson draws on the following source.

_items.title: See pages 200 to 202 of Chapter 11, 'Creating Effective Presentations and Working in Groups', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Orientation
body: Group work is the part of university most students would happily skip. Your mark depends on others, personalities clash, and the effort can feel unevenly shared. Yet it is also the closest rehearsal your degree offers for professional life, where almost nothing worthwhile is done alone. This lesson is about getting the most from it rather than merely surviving it.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level the aim is not just to contribute, but to see group work as tutors and employers see it. They are watching how you work with others, not only what the team produces. Understanding that shift in focus is what lets you turn a frustrating task into evidence of the skills a graduate needs.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain why tutors value the process of group work more than its end product
distinguish truly listening to a team member from merely hearing them in a worked example
identify the behaviour a group-work situation in {{context}} is calling for.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Tutors set group work to develop the interpersonal skills the workplace demands, so they are more interested in the process than the product. The mark reflects how well you worked together, not just the slides you produced. That is why a reflective account often forms part of the assessment: it asks you to evaluate how you communicated, listened, adapted and handled disagreement.

The behaviours tutors look for are the ones employers name too: communication and listening, collaboration, flexibility, resilience, leadership and accountability. Listening is the one most often missed. Hearing a team member means registering what they said; listening means thinking about it and doing something with it, even when you do not agree.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about a group you have worked in recently. When a teammate said something you disagreed with, did you really listen, or just wait for your turn? What is one behaviour from this lesson you could bring to your next group?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Group work is assessed for its process as much as its product, because that is where the skills employers want are built. You can now explain why tutors value the process, tell real listening apart from merely hearing, and name the behaviour a situation is calling for. The next lesson looks at what happens when a team falls into conflict, and how to reflect on it.

instruction: This lesson draws on the following source.

_items.title: See pages 212 to 215 of Chapter 11, 'Creating Effective Presentations and Working in Groups', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Orientation
body: Even a committed team runs into conflict, and how you handle it is often what the assessment is really testing. This lesson looks at two things that mark out an advanced learner: using an awareness of different personalities to work through a dispute, and being able to say, afterwards, what the whole experience was worth. Both turn a stressful task into something you can learn from and talk about.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are not expected to be a trained mediator. The aim is to recognise that people approach a task differently, to use that insight to calm a disagreement rather than inflame it, and to reflect honestly on your own part. This is the self-aware, articulate finalist that tutors and employers are looking for.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: use an awareness of personality types to choose a way through a group conflict
tell a reflective judgement about your own performance apart from a plain description of events
articulate the transferable-skills value of presenting and group work in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
One way to handle conflict in a team is to understand that people are built differently. The OCEAN model names five broad personality factors: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism. Roughly, these map to the innovator, the organiser, the communicator, the mediator and the realist. Recognising which tendency is driving a teammate, and which is driving you, helps you respond to the person rather than only to the position.

The second mark of an advanced learner is reflection that judges rather than describes. Saying what happened in a group is description. Saying what you did well, what you would change, and what the experience is worth to you as a graduate is a judgement. That judgement is where presenting and group work pay off: they build the communication, collaboration and resilience that employers call transferable skills.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about a disagreement in a team you were part of. What personality differences might have been behind it, and did you help resolve it or stay out of the way? If you had to tell an employer what that experience taught you, what would you say?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Handling conflict well starts with recognising that people differ, and using that awareness to find a way through rather than taking sides. Reflecting well means judging your performance, not just describing events, and naming what you have gained. You can now do both, and articulate the transferable-skills value of presenting and group work. With authority, collaboration and reflection in place, you are ready to present and work in teams like a graduate.

This is the test for the whole course. It covers everything you've studied in the lessons, with a set of questions to work through.

To pass, you need to score at least 70%. You can retake the test if you don't pass first time.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Presenting and group work are no longer just tasks to get through. You can present with authority, owning your material and defending your argument when it is challenged. You can collaborate the way tutors and employers value, listening as well as hearing, and taking real responsibility. And you can work through conflict using an awareness of personality, then reflect in a way that judges rather than describes and names what you have gained. Look back at the confidence check to see how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, authority and collaboration are things you practise in every module and every job. Each presentation you own rather than recite, each team you listen within rather than merely join, each conflict you steer rather than avoid, builds the graduate identity employers are looking for. The ability to communicate with authority and work well with others travels into every profession you might enter.

title: Course Sources
instruction: This course draws on the following source.

_items.title: See pages 200 to 219 of Chapter 11, 'Creating Effective Presentations and Working in Groups', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Four marks of an authoritative presenter
body: Each card names something an authoritative presenter does that a merely competent one does not.
instruction: Read through the cards below.
ariaRegion: Information cards about presenting with authority.

_items.title: Own the material
_items.subtitle: Not just know it
_items.text: You know the argument well enough to speak to it in your own words, so a missing slide or a lost thread does not stop you.

_items.title: Speak, do not read
_items.subtitle: Eyes on the room
_items.text: Prompt cards are fine, but you look at your audience and talk to them. Reading aloud tells a room you do not trust yourself with the ideas.

_items.title: Welcome the hard question
_items.subtitle: The real test
_items.text: A challenge is a chance to show the argument is yours. You answer it directly, concede any fair point, and hold your position with reasons.

_items.title: A case, not a report
_items.subtitle: You are arguing
_items.text: You are not listing facts; you are making a case and asking the room to accept it. Authority is the earned confidence to put that case and defend it.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two finalists give the same ten-minute presentation and then take questions.

{{learner-a}} has learned the slides by heart and delivers them smoothly. When an audience member asks why a rival approach was not considered, {{learner-a}} repeats a point from an earlier slide and moves on. The talk was fluent, but the argument lived only on the slides. Under the first real challenge, there was nothing to draw on. This is delivery without authority.

{{learner-b}} delivers the same material and then meets the same question directly. {{learner-b}} acknowledges the rival approach, explains in a sentence why it was set aside, and concedes one point where it has merit. The room can see the argument is understood, not memorised. This is authority: the case is owned, and it holds up when pushed.

Both presented the same content. Only {{learner-b}} could defend it, and that is what the room reads as authority.

title: Building authority
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: These habits build the authority this lesson describes. Try them when you next prepare a talk.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Can I explain my main argument in one sentence, without my slides?
Have I rehearsed aloud until I can speak to each point rather than read it?
Have I listed the three hardest questions I could be asked, and prepared answers?
Do I know which point I would concede, and which I would defend?
Have I planned to look at the audience rather than the screen or my cards?
Does my talk make a case, rather than just report what I found?

title: Formative check: presenting with authority
displayTitle: Which statement best describes presenting with authority?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which statement best describes presenting with authority?

_items.text: Owning your material and standing behind your argument, including when it is questioned.
_items.feedback: Yes. Authority is owning the case and being able to defend it.

_items.text: Delivering your slides as smoothly and confidently as possible.
_items.feedback: Smooth delivery is not the same as authority; a fluent talk can still collapse under a question.

_items.text: Speaking louder and faster than you would in conversation.
_items.feedback: Volume and pace are not authority; owning the argument is.

_items.text: Including as much detail as the time limit allows.
_items.feedback: More detail does not create authority; owning and defending the case does.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Authority means owning your material and defending your argument, not simply delivering it smoothly.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about owning the argument and defending it, rather than style of delivery.
_incorrect.final: Authority means owning your material and standing behind your argument when questioned. Smoothness, volume and detail are not the same thing.

title: Formative check: recognising authority
displayTitle: In the worked example, what gave the second presenter authority that the first lacked?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What gave the second presenter authority that the first lacked?

_items.text: They answered the challenge directly, conceded a fair point, and defended their position with reasons.
_items.feedback: Yes. Meeting the question and defending the case is authority in action.

_items.text: They delivered the slides more smoothly than the first presenter.
_items.feedback: Both delivered smoothly; that is not what made the difference.

_items.text: They spoke for longer and included more detail.
_items.feedback: Length and detail did not give the second presenter authority; defending the argument did.

_items.text: They avoided the difficult question to stay on script.
_items.feedback: Avoiding the question is what the first presenter effectively did; it is the opposite of authority.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second presenter owned the argument and defended it when challenged.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second presenter DID with the hard question, not how they delivered the slides.
_incorrect.final: The second presenter had authority because they met the challenge directly, conceded a fair point, and defended their position. Delivery and length were not the difference.

title: Formative check: defending your argument
displayTitle: You are presenting on a topic in {{context}} and are asked a question that challenges your main claim. Which response shows authority?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which response to a challenging question shows authority?

_items.text: Acknowledge the challenge, give your reason for your position, and concede any fair point.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, that is how you defend an argument with authority.

_items.text: Repeat the relevant slide word for word and move on.
_items.feedback: Repeating a slide dodges the challenge rather than answering it.

_items.text: Agree with the questioner to avoid looking defensive.
_items.feedback: Abandoning your position at the first push is not authority; defending it with reasons is.

_items.text: Say the question is outside the scope of your talk.
_items.feedback: Deflecting a fair challenge suggests the argument is not really yours.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, authority means answering the challenge, giving your reasons, and conceding any fair point.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that engages the challenge with reasons, rather than dodging or caving.
_incorrect.final: Authority means acknowledging the challenge, defending your position with reasons, and conceding fair points. Repeating a slide, caving, or deflecting all show the argument is not owned.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: A group project, stage by stage
body: A group project moves through stages, and each one calls for a different behaviour. Reveal each stage to see what it asks of you.
instruction: Select each stage to reveal the behaviour it calls for. Work through all five.

_items.title: Agree the objective
_items.body: Early on, agree what the team is really for. Tutors assess the process, not just the product, so treat the shared goal, and how you reach it, as the point.

_items.title: Take a real role
_items.body: Share the work fairly and own your part. Accountability means doing your task as well as you would expect of others, not coasting on the group's mark.

_items.title: Communicate and listen
_items.body: This is where most marks are won or lost. Make your views clear, and listen to others: think about what they say and do something with it, even if you disagree.

_items.title: Adapt and stay resilient
_items.body: Plans slip and people fall behind. Flexibility means taking on a changed role when needed; resilience means staying focused on the task rather than the frustration.

_items.title: Reflect on the process
_items.body: When it is over, judge how you worked with others and what you gained. This reflection, not just the finished slides, is often what the assessment rewards.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students sit in the same group meeting, where a teammate proposes an unusual idea for the project.

{{learner-a}} hears the idea, says 'sure, whatever works', and goes back to their own section. The idea is neither built on nor challenged. Later {{learner-a}} complains that the project lacked direction. {{learner-a}} heard the teammate but did not listen, because nothing was done with the contribution. This is participation without collaboration.

{{learner-b}} hears the same idea and asks two questions about how it would work, then suggests a way to fold part of it into the plan. The teammate feels heard, and the project gains something. When a later task falls through because a member is ill, {{learner-b}} takes it on rather than let the team stall. This is collaboration: listening turned into action, with accountability.

Both were in the room. Only {{learner-b}} did the thing tutors are actually assessing.

title: Collaborating well
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: These moves show the behaviours tutors and employers value. Try them in your next group.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I made my own views clear, rather than going quiet?
When a teammate spoke, did I act on their point rather than just wait for my turn?
Have I taken on a fair share of the work and done it conscientiously?
When a plan slipped, did I adapt rather than complain?
Have I helped move a disagreement forward rather than let it fester?
Afterwards, have I reflected on how I worked with others, not just on the mark?

title: Formative check: process over product
displayTitle: Why do tutors value the process of group work more than its finished product?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why do tutors value the process of group work over the product?

_items.text: Because group work is set to build the interpersonal skills the workplace needs, which show in how you work together.
_items.feedback: Yes. The process is where communication, collaboration and resilience are developed and assessed.

_items.text: Because the finished product is usually too short to mark fairly.
_items.feedback: The reason is not about length; it is about the skills the process builds.

_items.text: Because tutors do not have time to assess the product closely.
_items.feedback: It is not about tutor time; it is about what group work is for.

_items.text: Because the product rarely counts towards the final grade.
_items.feedback: The product often does count; tutors simply value the process more because of what it develops.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Group work is set to develop workplace skills, which show in the process rather than the product.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what group work is actually for, beyond the finished slides.
_incorrect.final: Tutors value the process because group work is set to build interpersonal skills for the workplace. It is not about the product's length, grade weight, or marking time.

title: Formative check: listening versus hearing
displayTitle: In the worked example, what did the second student do that counts as listening rather than just hearing?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What did the second student do that counts as listening rather than hearing?

_items.text: Asked questions about the idea and folded part of it into the plan.
_items.feedback: Yes. Listening means doing something with what a teammate says.

_items.text: Nodded along and said the idea was fine before moving on.
_items.feedback: That is hearing without listening, which is what the first student did.

_items.text: Wrote the idea down to mention in the reflective account.
_items.feedback: Recording an idea is not the same as acting on it in the work.

_items.text: Waited politely until the teammate had finished speaking.
_items.feedback: Waiting your turn is not listening; acting on the contribution is.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student acted on the idea, which is what turns hearing into listening.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second student DID with the idea, not how politely they received it.
_incorrect.final: Listening meant asking about the idea and building part of it into the plan. Nodding, noting it down, or simply waiting are all closer to hearing.

title: Formative check: the behaviour called for
displayTitle: You are in a group project in {{context}} and a teammate proposes an idea you are unsure about. Which response best shows the behaviour tutors value?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which response best shows the behaviour tutors value?

_items.text: Ask how the idea would work, then build on the useful part or explain your concern with reasons.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, engaging with the idea is the collaboration tutors are assessing.

_items.text: Say nothing and quietly carry on with your own section.
_items.feedback: Going quiet avoids the collaboration the task is designed to assess.

_items.text: Agree immediately to avoid any friction in the group.
_items.feedback: Agreeing without thought is not real listening or collaboration.

_items.text: Dismiss the idea because it is not how you would do it.
_items.feedback: Dismissing a teammate's view out of hand is the opposite of what tutors value.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, engaging with the idea and responding with reasons is the collaboration tutors value.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that engages with the idea, rather than ignoring, caving to, or dismissing it.
_incorrect.final: The behaviour tutors value is engaging with the idea and responding with reasons. Going silent, agreeing to avoid friction, or dismissing it all fall short.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Five personalities in a team
body: The OCEAN model describes five broad personality factors. Reveal each one to see the tendency it names and how to work with it in a team.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all five.

_items.title: Openness: the innovator
_items.body: High openness shows up as creative, unexpected ideas. Give these teammates room to propose, but ask how an idea serves the shared goal so the team does not chase novelty for its own sake.

_items.title: Conscientiousness: the organiser
_items.body: Conscientious teammates keep the plan, the deadlines and the detail in order. Value that structure rather than dismissing it as fussiness; it is often what gets the project delivered.

_items.title: Extraversion: the communicator
_items.body: Extravert teammates drive discussion and energy. Lean on them to keep the team talking, but make sure quieter members are still drawn in and heard.

_items.title: Agreeableness: the mediator
_items.body: Agreeable teammates smooth tension and look for compromise. They are invaluable in a dispute, but take care that real disagreements are resolved rather than simply papered over.

_items.title: Neuroticism: the realist
_items.body: Teammates high in this factor notice risks and voice worries. Treat their caution as useful early warning rather than negativity, and it will strengthen the team's decisions.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students are in a team where the designer and the researcher are arguing hard over the slides, two days before the pitch.

{{learner-a}} finds the row stressful and stays quiet, hoping it will pass. Asked later to reflect, {{learner-a}} writes that 'there was a disagreement but we sorted it in the end'. The conflict was neither helped nor understood, and the reflection only describes what happened. Nothing was learned that could be carried into the next team.

{{learner-b}} sees that the designer is an innovator and the researcher a cautious realist, both right in part. {{learner-b}} acknowledges each view, then proposes a middle way that keeps a clear layout but adds one bold idea. Reflecting afterwards, {{learner-b}} writes that stepping in early, and naming the strengths on both sides, was what held the team together, and would do so again. That is a judgement, and it names a transferable skill.

Both saw the same argument. Only {{learner-b}} resolved it and learned something sayable from it.

title: Working through conflict and reflecting
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: These moves help you steer a conflict and reflect in a way that judges rather than describes.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I asked what personality difference might be behind the disagreement?
Have I acknowledged the fair point on each side before taking a view?
Did I propose a way forward rather than wait for the row to pass?
In my reflection, have I said what I did, not just what happened?
Have I named what I would do differently next time, and why?
Can I say what this experience is worth to me as a graduate?

title: Formative check: using personality awareness
displayTitle: A teammate keeps raising worst-case problems and slowing decisions. Using an awareness of personality types, what is the most constructive response?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the most constructive response to the cautious teammate?

_items.text: Treat their caution as useful early warning and address the risks they name.
_items.feedback: Yes. Reading the realist's caution as useful turns it into better decisions.

_items.text: Ask them to stop being negative so the team can move on.
_items.feedback: Labelling caution as negativity dismisses a tendency that can protect the team.

_items.text: Ignore them and let the more positive members decide.
_items.feedback: Ignoring a teammate wastes the early warning their caution offers.

_items.text: Take over the decision yourself to save time.
_items.feedback: Overriding the person does not use the insight that personalities differ.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Reading the realist's caution as useful lets you address risks rather than dismiss the person.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what an awareness of personality types would have you do with the caution, rather than against the person.
_incorrect.final: The constructive response treats the caution as useful early warning. Telling them to stop, ignoring them, or taking over all waste the insight.

title: Formative check: judgement versus description
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's reflection a judgement rather than a description?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's reflection a judgement rather than a description?

_items.text: It said what they did, why it worked, and what they would do again.
_items.feedback: Yes. Weighing your own actions and drawing a lesson is a judgement.

_items.text: It gave a fuller account of what happened in the meeting.
_items.feedback: A fuller account of events is still description, however detailed.

_items.text: It was longer than the first student's reflection.
_items.feedback: Length does not make a judgement; weighing and concluding do.

_items.text: It named the other team members and their roles.
_items.feedback: Naming who did what is description, not a judgement about your own performance.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The reflection judged the student's own actions and drew a lesson, which is more than description.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the reflection concluded about the student's own performance, not how much it described.
_incorrect.final: It was a judgement because it weighed what the student did, why it worked, and what they would repeat. A fuller or longer account of events is still description.

title: Formative check: articulating the value
displayTitle: How would you best articulate the transferable-skills value of a group presentation in {{context}} to an employer?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: How would you best articulate the transferable-skills value to an employer?

_items.text: Name the communication, collaboration and resilience it built, with an example of each.
_items.feedback: Yes. Naming the skills with evidence is how you articulate the value in {{context}}.

_items.text: Say that you got a good mark for the presentation.
_items.feedback: A mark is not a transferable skill; employers want the skills behind it.

_items.text: Explain how many slides the team produced and how long it took.
_items.feedback: The output is not the point; the skills you developed are.

_items.text: Mention that group work is a normal part of your course.
_items.feedback: That it happened says nothing about what you gained from it.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, you articulate the value by naming the skills and evidencing them.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Employers want the transferable skills and evidence, not the mark or the output.
_incorrect.final: You articulate the value by naming the communication, collaboration and resilience it built, with examples. Marks, outputs and the mere fact of group work do not show the skills.

body: What does it mean to present with authority?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does it mean to present with authority?

_items.text: To own your material and defend your argument, including when it is challenged.
_items.feedback: Yes. Authority is owning and defending the case.

_items.text: To deliver your slides as smoothly as possible.
_items.feedback: Smooth delivery is not the same as authority.

_items.text: To speak louder and faster than normal.
_items.feedback: Volume and pace are not authority.

_items.text: To fit in as much detail as the time allows.
_items.feedback: More detail is not authority.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Presenting with authority means owning and defending your argument.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about owning and defending the argument.

body: A presenter is asked a question that challenges their argument. Which response best shows authority?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which response to a challenge best shows authority?

_items.text: Answer directly, give reasons, and concede any fair point.
_items.feedback: Yes. Defending the case with reasons is authority.

_items.text: Repeat an earlier slide and move on.
_items.feedback: Repeating a slide dodges the challenge.

_items.text: Immediately agree to avoid seeming defensive.
_items.feedback: Caving at the first push is not authority.

_items.text: Say the question is out of scope.
_items.feedback: Deflecting a fair challenge shows the argument is not owned.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Answering with reasons and conceding fair points shows authority.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the response that engages the challenge with reasons.

body: Why do tutors treat the process of group work as more important than the finished product?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is the process of group work more important than the product?

_items.text: Because it builds the interpersonal skills the workplace needs.
_items.feedback: Yes. The process develops the skills employers want.

_items.text: Because the product is too short to mark.
_items.feedback: It is not about length.

_items.text: Because tutors lack time to assess the product.
_items.feedback: It is not about tutor time.

_items.text: Because the product rarely counts towards the grade.
_items.feedback: The product often counts; the process is valued for the skills it builds.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The process builds the workplace skills group work is set to develop.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what group work is for.

body: What is the difference between listening to a team member and merely hearing them?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the difference between listening and merely hearing?

_items.text: Listening means thinking about what they said and acting on it; hearing just registers it.
_items.feedback: Yes. Listening does something with the contribution.

_items.text: Listening means staying silent until they finish.
_items.feedback: Staying silent is not listening.

_items.text: Listening means writing down everything they say.
_items.feedback: Recording words is not acting on them.

_items.text: Listening means agreeing with whatever they propose.
_items.feedback: Agreeing is not the same as listening.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Listening means acting on what a teammate says, not just registering it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about doing something with the contribution.

body: An awareness of personality types helps you in a team mainly because it lets you...
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Awareness of personality types helps you mainly because it lets you...

_items.text: respond to the person behind a disagreement, not just the position.
_items.feedback: Yes. It helps you handle the people, not only the argument.

_items.text: decide which teammates are not worth listening to.
_items.feedback: It is not for writing people off.

_items.text: predict exactly what every teammate will do.
_items.feedback: It is a guide to tendencies, not a precise prediction.

_items.text: avoid having to compromise with anyone.
_items.feedback: It supports working with others, not avoiding compromise.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Awareness of personality helps you respond to the person, not just the position.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about responding to the people behind a disagreement.

body: Which of these is a reflective judgement about group work, rather than a description?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which of these is a reflective judgement rather than a description?

_items.text: Stepping in early to name each side's strengths was what held the team together.
_items.feedback: Yes. It weighs an action and draws a lesson.

_items.text: There was a disagreement about the slides two days before the pitch.
_items.feedback: That just reports what happened.

_items.text: The team had four members, each with a different role.
_items.feedback: That describes the set-up, not a judgement.

_items.text: We met on Monday and finished the slides on Wednesday.
_items.feedback: That is a timeline of events, not a judgement.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A judgement weighs what you did and draws a lesson from it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that weighs an action, rather than reporting events.

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: presenting with authority, collaborating well in a group, and handling conflict while reflecting on what the work is worth. On their own they are three separate ideas. This lesson brings them together into one practice of working with people.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage the aim is to see these three as one practice, rather than three separate ideas. Real work rarely asks for just one of them. A group presentation calls on all three at once, so the habit of using them together is what carries into the rest of your studies and your career.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: bring together presenting with authority, collaborating in a group, and reflecting to improve, as one practice of working with people
recognise all three working together in how a student handles a piece of group work
plan how you will bring the three together on your next piece of group or presentation work in {{context}}

title: Concept: definition
body: Working with people is one practice, not three separate skills. You present your own part with authority, you collaborate with the team around you, and you handle friction and reflect so the next time goes better. The three ideas from the earlier lessons are the parts of that one practice, and a real piece of work calls on them together.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, this means bringing all three together on real work, whatever the subject. You own your own part and present it with authority, you collaborate and listen within the team, and you steer any conflict rather than avoid it. Afterwards you reflect honestly and carry one change into the next piece of work. Over a term, treating these as one practice, rather than three separate skills, is what makes you someone others want to work with.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about a group project or presentation you have coming up in your studies. How will you bring authority, collaboration and reflection together on it, and where will you start?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Presenting and working with others are most useful when you treat them as one practice, not three separate skills. You bring authority, collaboration and reflection together on every piece of work, and carry one change into the next. It is this habit, built piece after piece, that makes you an effective and self-aware graduate.

title: The practice as one cycle
displayTitle: The practice as one cycle
body: Working with people is one continuing practice that feeds the next piece of work. Select each part to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each part of the cycle.

_items.title: Agree the goal
_items.body: Agree the team's shared goal and take a real role, doing your own part conscientiously.

_items.title: Own your part
_items.body: Prepare your section until you own it, so you can present it with authority and answer questions.

_items.title: Steer conflict
_items.body: When the team disagrees, use an awareness of personality to steer the conflict towards a fair way forward.

_items.title: Reflect
_items.body: Afterwards, reflect honestly on how you worked with others, and name what you would carry into the next piece of work.

_diagram.title: Working with people as a continuing practice

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body: Two students work on the same group presentation. Student A prepares their own slides well but stays quiet when the team disagrees, and afterwards only notes that 'it went fine'. Student B owns their section and defends it, listens and folds in a teammate's idea, steps in to steer a disagreement, and afterwards names what they would do differently next time. Both knew the material, but Student B brought authority, collaboration and reflection together, and the whole team felt it.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: Checklist: How to bring the three together
body: Use these to check you are working with people as one practice, not just part of it.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Did I prepare my own part well enough to present it with authority and defend it?
Did I listen to my teammates and act on what they said, not just hear them?
When a disagreement came up, did I use an awareness of personality to help steer it?
Afterwards, did I reflect with honest judgement rather than just describe what happened?
Have I named one thing I will carry into my next piece of group or presentation work?

displayTitle: Why is it more useful to treat presenting, collaborating and reflecting as one practice rather than three separate skills?
body: Why is it more useful to treat presenting, collaborating and reflecting as one practice rather than three separate skills?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to treat presenting, collaborating and reflecting as one practice rather than three separate skills?

_items.text: Because real work calls on all three at once: a group presentation needs authority, collaboration and honest reflection together.
_items.feedback: Yes. The three connect, so using them as one habit is what makes you effective with people.

_items.text: Because being good at one of them means you can skip the other two.
_items.feedback: No. The point is that the three connect, not that any one replaces the rest.

_items.text: Because it means you never have to work in a team or take questions.
_items.feedback: Not so. Collaboration and defending your argument are parts of the practice, not things it removes.

_items.text: Because one practice is quicker to learn than three separate skills.
_items.feedback: The gain is not speed. It is that the three support one another in real work.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Presenting, collaborating and reflecting are one practice whose parts support one another.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how a single piece of group work needs all three at the same time.

displayTitle: In a group presentation, a student owns their section and defends it, listens and adapts with the team, helps steer a disagreement, then reflects honestly afterwards. What does this show?
body: In a group presentation, a student owns their section and defends it, listens and adapts with the team, helps steer a disagreement, then reflects honestly afterwards. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: In a group presentation, a student owns their section and defends it, listens and adapts with the team, helps steer a disagreement, then reflects honestly afterwards. What does this show?

_items.text: That the student is using presenting, collaborating and reflecting as one practice of working with people.
_items.feedback: Yes. All three are there, working together on the same piece of work.

_items.text: That the student is doing more than any one piece of group work really needs.
_items.feedback: No. Each part does a different job, and together they make the work stronger.

_items.text: That only the reflection at the end really mattered.
_items.feedback: Not so. The authority and collaboration did the real work, and reflection improves the next round.

_items.text: That presenting and collaborating are the same thing.
_items.feedback: They are different parts of the one practice, used together rather than merged.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The student brought all three together on one piece of work.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Notice how the student uses authority, collaboration and reflection at the same time.

displayTitle: You want to use this whole practice to work better with others in {{context}} this term. Which plan best treats presenting, collaborating and reflecting as one practice?
body: You want to use this whole practice to work better with others in {{context}} this term. Which plan best treats presenting, collaborating and reflecting as one practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to use this whole practice to work better with others in your subject this term. Which plan best treats presenting, collaborating and reflecting as one practice?

_items.text: On each piece of group or presentation work, own your part, collaborate and listen, steer any conflict, then reflect on what to carry forward.
_items.feedback: Yes. That brings all three together, in order, every time you work with others.

_items.text: Focus only on presenting your own part well, and leave the teamwork to look after itself.
_items.feedback: That drops collaboration and reflection, which is where much of the work with people happens.

_items.text: Avoid group work whenever you can, so there is no conflict to handle.
_items.feedback: Avoiding teams means you never build the practice the course is about.

_items.text: Reflect at the end of term, but do not change how you work along the way.
_items.feedback: Reflection only helps if you carry a change into the next piece of work.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Used together on every piece of work, the three are one practice.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the plan that brings all three together, not just one.

title: Summative item 7 (tests co4)
displayTitle: Which of these best describes what this course has taught about presenting and working with others?
body: Which of these best describes what this course has taught about presenting and working with others?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which of these best describes what this course has taught about presenting and working with others?

_items.text: They are one practice: present with authority, collaborate well, handle conflict, and reflect to improve.
_items.feedback: Yes. The three strands are one connected practice.

_items.text: They are a single talent that some people are born with and others are not.
_items.feedback: No. They are a practice you can learn and keep improving.

_items.text: They are three separate skills that have nothing to do with one another.
_items.feedback: The three connect: a real piece of work needs them together.

_items.text: They are mostly about speaking loudly and confidently.
_items.feedback: Confidence of delivery is not the same as authority, collaboration and reflection.

_feedback.correct: Correct.

title: Summative item 8 (tests co4)
displayTitle: A student has a new group presentation to prepare. Which approach uses the whole practice this course describes?
body: A student has a new group presentation to prepare. Which approach uses the whole practice this course describes?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student has a new group presentation to prepare. Which approach uses the whole practice this course describes?

_items.text: Own their section with authority, collaborate and listen with the team, steer any disagreement, then reflect afterwards.
_items.feedback: Yes. All three strands, used together on one piece of work.

_items.text: Prepare their own slides perfectly and ignore how the team is working.
_items.feedback: This drops collaboration and reflection, which the practice depends on.

_items.text: Let the most confident member make every decision to avoid conflict.
_items.feedback: Avoiding conflict is not the same as steering it well.

_items.text: Wait until the mark comes back before thinking about how it went.
_items.feedback: Reflection helps most when you carry a change into the next piece of work.

_feedback.correct: Correct.
